section_summary: This section continues a wartime report alleging systematic Japanese propaganda, economic penetration, espionage, and invasion planning in the Netherlands East Indies. It describes the use of fishermen, government-backed companies, consulates, commercial firms, local associations, military visitors, and the Kobayashi Mission to gather intelligence and prepare political and economic control. Pages 57–66 reproduce nine supporting documents, including propaganda plans, intelligence reports, corporate correspondence, sabotage instructions, a spy's letter, and a roster of visiting Japanese officers and aliases.

subfiles.title: Japanese Aggression: propaganda, economic assault, espionage, and preparations for invasion
subfiles.about: Continuation of a report alleging coordinated Japanese propaganda, economic penetration, intelligence collection, and preparations to invade and administer the Netherlands East Indies.
subfiles.summary: The report first describes Japanese contacts with Indonesian nationalists, rumor campaigns, radio propaganda, and the use of fishermen as naval auxiliaries and intelligence collectors. It then examines government-backed colonization, shipping, plantation, forestry, mining, airline, and trading enterprises whose allegedly commercial activities placed Japanese personnel near strategic ports, oilfields, and sea routes. Later sections describe consular espionage networks, commercial and community participation, military reconnaissance, the concealed objectives of the Kobayashi Mission, press agitation, deliberate provocations, and plans for governing occupied territory. The discovery of occupation plans and military intelligence in Consul Masaji Nonomura's archives is presented as confirmation of the report's allegations.

subfiles.title: Document I: Plan for the Publication of a Daily Paper in the Malay Language by Japanese in the Netherlands Indies
subfiles.from: T. Kotani and an unstated project author
subfiles.about: Proposal to establish a Japanese-financed Malay daily newspaper at Batavia for political propaganda and commercial influence.
subfiles.summary: Kotani's accompanying note forwards the project and wishes Kaneko success. The plan proposes Saeroen as chief editor, Tatsuji Kubo as adviser, and Tatsuo Mominoki as translator of Japanese news, with publication at Batavia and a circulation target of 5,000. Its budget anticipates an initial outlay of 31,000 guilders and a small monthly deficit. The authors argue that a Malay paper would counter Chinese reporting, publicize Japanese commerce, and advance Japan's southward policy among the indigenous population.

subfiles.title: Document II: Letter from Keizo Kaneko to Tatsuji Kubo on financing underground activities
subfiles.about: Kaneko discusses financing, personnel, and alternatives for establishing a Japanese-backed Malay propaganda newspaper in the Netherlands Indies.
subfiles.summary: Kaneko laments the failure to begin publication but promises continued financial support even if he and Mominoki remain barred from the Netherlands Indies. He identifies funds from Yosuke Matsuoka, the East Asiatic Economic Research Bureau, and Ainosuke Iwata, and suggests buying and transferring Sinar Selatan if a new paper cannot be founded. He asks Kubo to coordinate closely with the Foreign Ministry and consulate-general, support Saeroen and Mrs. Mominoki, and remain committed to state service. Kaneko also reports planned travel through Taiwan, Xiamen, Guangzhou, and Hong Kong.

subfiles.title: Document III: Japanese agents' party for Javanese political leaders
subfiles.about: Identification of Japanese agents who attended a Surabaya gathering intended to cultivate Javanese political extremists.
subfiles.summary: The document describes a party given at Surabaya by Japanese agents seeking cooperation with Javanese extremist leaders. It identifies Tatsuo Mominoki, Kinichi Takenaka, E. Hachisuwa, Hiroshi Kubota, Takekoshi, and Keizo Kaneko, noting the espionage or commercial affiliations of several participants.

subfiles.title: Document IV: Report by T. Yoshizumi on propaganda among Chinese residents
subfiles.to: Ataru Toyoshima, for the Japanese consul-general
subfiles.about: Yoshizumi recommends reframing Japanese propaganda to appeal jointly to Chinese and Indonesians in the Netherlands Indies under the slogan of Asian solidarity.
subfiles.summary: Yoshizumi argues that propaganda directed at Chinese residents cannot simply reproduce Japan's approach in China because both locally born Peranakans and China-born Sinkehs have deep interests in the Netherlands Indies. He advises placing the construction of a Japanese-led new Asian order before the settlement of the Sino-Japanese conflict. The proposed appeal would emphasize alleged common oppression of Chinese and Indonesians and promote the slogan of Asia for Asians. He expects Japanese imperial ideology to weaken Chinese identification with the Indies and facilitate cooperation under Japanese leadership.

subfiles.title: Document V: Letter from Yoshio Inoue on Palau and expansion toward New Guinea
subfiles.to: Manager of the Nanyo Kohatsu Kaisha at Momi, New Guinea
subfiles.about: A company manager reports strategic infrastructure and personnel measures supporting Japanese expansion from Palau toward New Guinea.
subfiles.summary: Inoue describes commercial and research ventures in the Spratly Islands and Hainan, while arguing that Japan must obtain tropical raw materials through the expansion of its nationals into New Guinea. He reports that the Tokyo–Palau airline is flown by active naval officers and notes construction of a large quay and two 10,000-ton oil tanks at Palau. Naval officials are said to be assisting the company's New Guinea enterprise. Permission for ten additional employees is portrayed as requiring exceptionally capable men who could serve as pioneers of expansion.

subfiles.title: Document VI: Haruji Matsue's instructions for clandestine oil exploration in New Guinea
subfiles.doc_type: corporate directive with reproduction and translation
subfiles.from: Haruji Matsue, co-signed by Mizuno Tsunemichi and Bunya Saito
subfiles.about: The Nanyo Kohatsu president directs secret investigation of land and legal procedures for a proposed New Guinea oil company.
subfiles.summary: Matsue forwards reports from the Japanese Naval Staff and the consulate-general at Batavia concerning a New Guinea oil company. He orders Kosugi to study Netherlands Indies mining law and secretly investigate approximately 1.7 million hectares of mapped territory, including procedures for applications and experimental drilling. A note records that Consul-General Koshida supplied mining legislation and that Naval Staff information drew on Foreign Ministry reporting about the Netherlands New Guinea Petroleum Company.

subfiles.title: Document VII: Chuang Kung Ming's report on espionage, sabotage, and fifth-column organization
subfiles.doc_type: intelligence letter with reproduction and translation
subfiles.to: President Sukihara and Kyujiro Hayashi via the Japanese Association at Batavia
subfiles.about: A Penang-based intelligence agent reports clandestine recruitment, espionage, sabotage preparations, rumor spreading, and efforts to corrupt soldiers and civilians.
subfiles.summary: Chuang states that he has intensified his work under instructions from the Overseas Intelligence Bureau and established contact with agents operating separately in Thailand. Their assigned tasks include recruiting confederates, committing sabotage, inciting indigenous hostility, and spreading alarming rumors. He reports funding for bribing soldiers and civilians and for organizing a fifth column ready for wartime action. Hayashi's arrival at Batavia is expected to produce more extensive and definite instructions.

subfiles.title: Document VIII: Hiroshi Kubota's letter on military and pan-Asian contacts
subfiles.about: Kubota reports confidential meetings with Japanese military authorities and plans to mobilize Japanese residents of the Netherlands Indies through the Meijikai.
subfiles.summary: Kubota recounts meetings in Taipei, Kobe, and Tokyo with the General Staff, naval and gendarmerie officials, admirals, a lieutenant-general, journalists, and southward-expansion organizations. He says he publicly advocated opening the South and received introductions and lengthy private interviews with prominent figures. Kubota proposes enrolling all Japanese residents in the Netherlands Indies in the Meijikai, collecting subscriptions, publishing pamphlets, briefing visitors, and sending representatives to Japan. Although immediate financial assistance remained uncertain, he expected support after the organization demonstrated activity.

subfiles.title: Document IX: Officers who visited the Netherlands Indies in 1940
subfiles.about: Roster of Japanese military visitors, retired officers, company advisers, and intelligence operatives who travelled under false identities.
subfiles.summary: The document lists twenty-four serving army and navy officers who visited the Netherlands Indies during 1940, including Mamoru Ōta, Yasuto Nakayama, Tadashi Maeda, and other senior officers. It separately identifies retired admirals and a retired colonel travelling for business, study, or instructional purposes. A final table connects several false names and pretended occupations with the alleged real identities and functions of shipping executives, spies, a General Staff colonel, and a naval commander.
